story.title: Landslide at Guinea Landfill Claims 31 Lives
story.summary: A landslide at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, has resulted in the deaths of at least 31 people. The incident occurred after heavy rains caused a mound of rubbish to collapse, burying nearby homes and tents. This disaster follows recent government announcements regarding plans to relocate the waste site due to safety concerns, particularly during the rainy season.

explore_lenses.label: Why is this more than a single landslide?
explore_lenses.title: A chronic waste and housing risk
explore_lenses.summary: The collapse exposed a longstanding overlap of waste disposal, informal housing and livelihoods at Dar-es-Salam, Conakry's largest open-air landfill. The immediate death toll is only part of the public-safety issue because residents and waste pickers remained exposed to hazards before the collapse.

claims.text: Dar-es-Salam is Conakry's largest landfill, and heavy rain triggered the collapse that buried nearby shacks and destroyed homes.
Local reporting before the disaster documented homes close to the waste mound, runoff moving through refuse toward inhabited areas, and people working on the dump to recover recyclable materials.

Residents had raised health concerns about smoke, odors and runoff, but the local report said medical assessment would be needed to establish any scientific link between reported illnesses and landfill exposure.

explore_lenses.label: How did the danger persist until the collapse?
explore_lenses.title: Warnings and closure plans came too late
explore_lenses.summary: The landfill's risks were known before August 23: Guinea's disaster-risk strategy explicitly lists landfill-waste collapse as a hazard, and local reporting documented the site's proximity to homes. Authorities say they had urged residents to leave, while a local activist argues the state failed to close the site despite earlier promises.

claims.text: Guinea's 2024-2030 national disaster-risk-reduction strategy identifies both landslides and collapses of waste at landfills among hazards the country faces.
Local reporting said a technical mission had begun to prepare Dar-es-Salam's closure and rehabilitation, but the collapse occurred before the closure was effective.

Minister Dienabou Touré said authorities had repeatedly sought to move residents because of the area's health and safety risks; civil-society leader Ange Gabriel Haba called for the state to use its authority to remove people from collapse-prone sites.

Resident activist Abou Hamza said neighbors had organized protests and invited responsible services, and he held the state responsible for not taking the necessary steps to close the dump despite what he described as a year-old promise.

explore_lenses.label: What happens to survivors and the landfill now?
explore_lenses.title: Rescue, relocation and a difficult closure
explore_lenses.summary: Authorities' immediate tasks are searching the unstable debris, treating the injured and relocating remaining families. Longer term, closing Dar-es-Salam requires both securing the existing waste mound and finding an alternative destination for Conakry's daily waste.

claims.text: The government said its August 23 provisional tally was 30 deaths, six seriously injured people and 16 lightly injured people, with medical care arranged at Donka University Hospital.
Search-and-rescue operations were continuing for possible survivors, and the government said it had deployed personnel and equipment to recover victims and assist those affected.
Touré said remaining families would be relocated; authorities said many residents had already received eviction notices, but others were still present when the collapse occurred.
Local reporting assessed that effective closure will require securing and treating the existing dump while establishing a durable alternative for the waste generated daily in Conakry.

story_report.summary: Heavy rain triggered the collapse of a waste mound at the Dar-es-Salam landfill in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and shacks. At least 31 people have been reported dead, while the government’s August 23 provisional count listed 30 deaths, six people seriously injured and 16 with lighter injuries. Rescue teams continued searching for possible survivors as authorities deployed personnel and equipment to recover victims and assist residents affected by the disaster.

sections.heading: Dar-es-Salam Landfill Risks
sections.body: Dar-es-Salam is Conakry’s largest landfill. Reporting before the collapse documented housing close to the waste mound, runoff passing through refuse toward inhabited areas, and people recovering recyclable materials at the site. Residents had raised concerns about smoke, odours and runoff, although the reported illnesses and any scientific link to landfill exposure have not been medically established.

sections.heading: Closure Plans and Responsibility
sections.body: The government had planned to relocate the landfill because of safety concerns, and a technical mission had begun preparations for its closure and rehabilitation before the collapse. Minister Dienabou Touré said authorities had repeatedly sought to move residents from the area; resident activist Abou Hamza said neighbours had protested and faulted the state for failing to close the dump despite a promise he described as a year old. Guinea’s disaster-risk strategy identifies landfill waste collapses and landslides as hazards facing the country.

sections.heading: Relocation and Waste Disposal
sections.body: Touré said remaining families would be relocated, while authorities said many residents had already received eviction notices but others were still at the site when the mound gave way. Local reporting said an effective closure would require securing and treating the existing dump as well as creating a durable alternative for the waste generated each day in Conakry. The consulted reporting did not set out a timetable, relocation details or a confirmed replacement disposal site.

unresolved.text: The final death toll remains unsettled: the government’s August 23 statement described its count as provisional, while other reporting put the number of deaths at at least 31.
No consulted source establishes the final cause of the collapse or legal responsibility; an investigation or technical assessment would be needed.

related_stories.summary: A fast-moving wildfire in northwest Reno, Nevada, has prompted authorities to urge the evacuation of approximately 90,000 residents. The fire, which has destroyed homes and complicated firefighting efforts due to shifting winds, has also endangered first responders and civilians. Fire crews are struggling to control the blaze as it jumps over fire trucks and creates hazardous conditions.
